parts:
How are you comparing speed? The only measure that makes
sense is effective samples per second (or seconds per effective
sample).

If you can share the Stan model, we could tell you more.
There are various "tricks" to implementing such models having
to do with reparameterizations --- there's a discussion in the manual,
which also has a pointer to the Betancourt and Girolami arXiv paper, with
a much deeper analysis of hierarchical models in HMC.

- Bobp

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Takes so much time to estimate Hierarchical Model compared with Bayesm package
parts:
The number of iterations is irrelevant. It's the number
of *effective samples* divided by time that matters.
The reason this matters is that the standard error on your
posterior mean estimates is posterior std deviation divided
by the square root of the number of effective samples.

You only need to run until you get the standard error down
to reasonable levels.

Are you running the four chains in parallel?

What do you mean by "conducted in different condition"? Is
it the same model and same data?

Do you know what kind of sampling they use in bayesm? The
CRAN pages says to see their book, and the book table of
contents describes Gibbs, Metropolis and Hybrid (presumably
same as Hamiltonian, but I couldn't tell from the contents).

Now getting to your model:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> L;
int<lower=0> n_smp_id;
int<lower=0> n_smp_id2;
int<lower=0,upper=n_smp_id> smp_id[N]; //defining ID
int<lower=0,upper=n_smp_id2> smp_id2[L]; //defining ID
vector[N] y;
vector[N] x1;
int<lower=0> M;
matrix[L,M] x2;
}

parameters {
vector[n_smp_id] a;
vector[n_smp_id] b;
vector[n_smp_id2] mu_a;
vector[n_smp_id2] mu_b;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id] sig_y;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id2] sig_a;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id2] sig_b;
vector[M] theta;
}

//letting variance as uniform
transformed parameters {
vector[N] y_hat;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[N] sig_y_hat;
vector[L] mu_a_hat;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id2] sig_a_hat;
vector[L] mu_b_hat;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id2] sig_b_hat;

for (i in 1:N) {
y_hat[i] <- a[smp_id[i]] + b[smp_id[i]] * x1[i];
sig_y_hat[i] <- sig_y[smp_id[i]];
}

for (j in 1:L) {
mu_a_hat[j] <- 0;
sig_a_hat[j] <- 100;
mu_b_hat[j] <- x2[j]*theta;
sig_b_hat[j] <- 100; //sig_b[smp_id2[j]]
}

}

model {
mu_a ~ normal(0,1);

a ~ normal(mu_a_hat, sig_a_hat);
b ~ normal(mu_b_hat, sig_b_hat);
y ~ normal(y_hat, sig_y_hat);
}


You don't need to assign constants to transformed parameters,
and there's no need to repeat given Stan's vectorization.
You should find a substantial speedup if you change

transformed parameters {
...
vector[L] mu_a_hat;
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[n_smp_id2] sig_a_hat;

for (j in 1:L) {
...
mu_a_hat[j] <- 0;
sig_a_hat[j] <- 100;
...
}

}

model {
...
a ~ normal(mu_a_hat, sig_a_hat);
...

to

model {
...
a ~ normal(0, 100);
}

and similarly for mu_b_hat and sig_b_hat. (I also wouldn't
use "hat" in the variable names, as it's usually reserved
for point estimates.)

As far as I can tell, you're not even using mu_a or sig_a
in the model other than as mu_a ~ normal(0,1), so I think
you can just drop mu_a as a parameter and this sampling statement.

But what's really going to slow your model down more than all
of this is that you define a parameter

vector[n_smp_id2] mu_b;

and never use it. This leads to an improper prior (uniform on
the reals), which is impossible to sample from (not just for
Stan, but for anything).

Try cleaning these up and rerun for a couple hundred iterations
and see what happens.

- Bob
